217 - The Philosophy of Clint Eastwood: Clint Eastwood is one of American cinema's most durable figures, first as the squinting gunslinger of the spaghetti westerns and Dirty Harry, then for five decades as a director of spare dramas like Unforgiven, Million Dollar Baby, and Gran Torino. This book argues Eastwood practices philosophy on film: his characters face stark moral choices, questions of fate and self-reliance, justice beyond the law, and evil and suffering without easy answers. The essays read him through Aristotle, the Stoics, Nietzsche, and the problem of evil.
218 - The Philosophy of the Coen Brother: Joel and Ethan Coen make darkly comic American films, including Fargo, The Big Lebowski, No Country for Old Men, and Blood Simple, where ordinary people meet catastrophe and nonsense. Their world of failed plans, coin-flipping hitmen, and accidental survivors raises real questions: whether life is governed by fate or chance, whether nihilism can actually be lived, what shame and virtue look like in small-town America, and why we laugh at misery. The essays answer with Nietzsche, Aristotle, Kierkegaard, and theories of comedy.
219 - The Philosophy of David Cronenberg: David Cronenberg is the Canadian director who built a career on body horror: The Fly, Videodrome, Dead Ringers, eXistenZ, and A History of Violence. His films break bodies and boundaries apart, which makes them natural philosophy problems: is a teleported person still you, where does a mind end and its technology begin, why does the human body disgust us, and can a killer shed his old identity like skin? The essays bring Descartes, Locke, Wittgenstein, and Aristotle to bear on the flesh.
220 - The Philosophy of David Lynch: David Lynch is the American filmmaker of the strange, from Eraserhead to Mulholland Drive, and co-creator of Twin Peaks, the 1990 television series about an FBI agent investigating a homecoming queen's murder in a logging town where the woods hide something evil. The essays use Lynch to ask how we can know anything, weighing Cooper's dreams and intuitions against scientific certainty, alongside questions of the self, Kantian aesthetics, doppelgangers, and why his images seem to mean more than they say.
221 - The Philosophy of Film Noir: Film noir is the dark Hollywood crime style of the 1940s and 50s, seen in The Maltese Falcon, Double Indemnity, and Out of the Past, with its private eyes, femme fatales, and doomed men. Its world of betrayed values and shadowed motives is why it merits a philosophy book: the essays connect noir to existentialism and to Nietzsche's death of God, Camus's absurd, reason against passion, and the question of whether objective morality survives when the guilty walk away free.
222 - The Philosophy of Horror: Horror here means horror rooted in women's reproductive bodies: menstruation, virginity, pregnancy, motherhood, and menopause in films from Rosemary's Baby and Alien to Carrie and Teeth. The essays coin the term gynaehorror and ask why the genre both polices and disturbs femininity, reading it through Foucault, Kristeva, Deleuze, and feminist theory to show how horror films enforce impossible ideals of motherhood and sexuality, and how they can also turn those ideals inside out.
223 - The Philosophy of J.J. Abrams: Though this volume's title names J.J. Abrams, its essays all concern Stanley Kubrick, the exacting director of 2001: A Space Odyssey, Dr. Strangelove, A Clockwork Orange, The Shining, and Eyes Wide Shut. Kubrick's films follow soldiers, boxers, astronauts, and husbands confronting a cold universe that supplies no ready-made meanings, which is why they invite philosophy. The essays read his whole career as a cinematic existentialism, drawing on Camus, Nietzsche, Heidegger, and Kierkegaard on absurdity, freedom, and death.
224 - The Philosophy of Joss Whedon: Joss Whedon created Buffy the Vampire Slayer and Angel, the space western Firefly, and Dollhouse, and co-wrote Marvel's Avengers films. His ensembles of slayers, soulful vampires, and malfunctioning dolls are built for philosophical work: can a soul be re-ensouled, are Angel and Angelus one person or two, do his heroes possess genuinely free will, and can a screen show arguments that no paraphrase captures? The essays deploy Heidegger, Rawls, Locke, and Parfit, arguing Whedon does not merely illustrate philosophy but does it.
225 - The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese: Martin Scorsese, the director of Taxi Driver, Goodfellas, Raging Bull, and Casino, has spent fifty years filming violent men who cannot be at peace. That fixation is why he merits a philosophy book: Taxi Driver asks when vigilantism is justified, Goodfellas stages Plato's old challenge of why one should be just when crime pays, and Casino tests whether an egoist can have a real friend. The essays bring Aristotle, Plato, Nietzsche, and Scorsese's own Catholic guilt to bear on his characters' unhappy souls.
226 - The Philosophy of Michael Mann: Michael Mann makes sleek crime films, including Thief, Manhunter, Heat, and Collateral, about professionals with codes: master thieves, criminal profilers, a hitman who works nights. His loners, weighing love against work in glass-and-steel cities, are existentialist figures, and that is the thread of this book: freedom and authenticity, Sartre's condemnation to choose, Nietzschean will to power in men who fight monsters, and whether the outsider who refuses to belong can still be good. The essays read Mann through Camus, Nietzsche, and Levinas.
